summary: Evidence is mixed and mostly adjacent. Human readability and maintenance studies justify monitoring code shape, while newer agent research shows that dependency complexity and context selection matter more than any universal file, function or method limit.

items.text: Buse and Weimer, Learning a Metric for Code Readability (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 2010), learned from 120 human annotators, predicted readability judgments with about 80% accuracy and found correlations with changes and defect indicators over more than 2.2 million lines. It supports measurable local readability, but correlation does not identify a causal line-count threshold.

Basili, Briand and Melo, A Validation of Object-Oriented Design Metrics as Quality Indicators (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 1996), analyzed eight systems built from identical requirements and found several class design metrics useful for predicting fault-prone classes. It supports bounding complex class surfaces, while the C++ student-project setting limits transfer to modern agent workflows.

Palomba, Bavota, Di Penta, Fasano, Oliveto and De Lucia, On the Diffuseness and the Impact on Maintainability of Code Smells (Empirical Software Engineering, 2018), examined 395 releases and 13 smell types, finding long or complex smells widespread and smelly classes more change- and fault-prone. This is observational evidence and does not prove that mechanically splitting files improves quality.

Zhang et al., Hierarchical Context Pruning: Optimizing Real-World Code Completion with Repository-Level Pretrained Code LLMs (Chinese Academy of Sciences and partners, AAAI 2025), evaluated hierarchical pruning across repository-level code-completion models and reported improved completion after removing irrelevant context. This directly supports selective model context, but not source-code size caps as the pruning mechanism.

Rando et al., LongCodeBench (2025 preprint), found that longer individual files correlated with higher QA accuracy for Gemini 2 Flash in five of six context brackets. This is observational and does not imply that larger files cause better results; it does refute a universal smaller-file rule.

Wang et al., CodeFlowBench (ACL 2026), found lower model performance as dependency complexity rose in multi-turn code tasks. This supports checking coupling and change scope rather than enforcing physical length caps.
